title: Softmax Regression (Multinomial Logistic Regression)
abstract:
Logistic regression handles two classes. When there are more — Yes / No /
Opt-out — the model computes one score per class and the softmax function turns
those scores into probabilities that sum to one. This document covers the
construction, proves that softmax reduces to the sigmoid when there are two
classes, derives the cross-entropy loss and its remarkably clean gradient,
explains the shift-invariance that both causes the redundancy in the parameters
and provides the numerical-stability fix, and contrasts it with the one-vs-rest
alternative.

blocks.t: The Setup
From the notes

items:
Till now we studied logistic regression in a binary setup
 $\{0,1\}$.

Now we have more than 2, e.g. Yes / No / Opt-out
 classes in the output.
For each class the model computes a score $z_1,z_2,z_3$.

Softmax converts these scores to probabilities between 0 and 1,
 e.g. $[0.2,\ 0.7,\ 0.2]$.
Pick the class with the highest probability for each point.

For each point the model computes probabilities of all 3 classes
 and picks the one class with the highest probability.

blocks.cap:
The pipeline. One linear score per class, softmax to convert them into
 a probability distribution, and argmax to pick the winner.

blocks.t: The Formula
Scores, then softmax

Each class $c$ gets its own weight vector, so the parameters form a matrix
$W\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times p}$ and a bias vector $b\in\mathbb{R}^{C}$:
z_c = w_c^{ \top}x+b_c,\qquad c=1,\ldots,C .
Then
and the prediction is $\hat y=\arg\max_c P(y=c\mid x)$.
Why exponentiate, then normalise

Two requirements must be met for the output to be a probability distribution:
every entry non-negative, and the entries summing to 1.

items:
$e^{z}$ makes every term positive, whatever sign the score has.
 Normalising the raw scores would fail as soon as one was negative.
Dividing by the sum forces $\sum_c p_c=1$ by construction.

Exponentiating also amplifies differences: a score gap of 2 becomes
 a probability ratio of $e^2\approx7.4$. Hence "soft-max" — a smooth,
 differentiable approximation to picking the maximum.

blocks.t: Softmax Generalises the Sigmoid
The two-class case
With $C=2$,
Divide numerator and denominator by $e^{z_1}$:

Softmax with two classes is the sigmoid, applied to the
difference of the two scores. Binary logistic regression is the special
case in which we fix $z_0=0$ and keep only one weight vector — which is exactly
what makes it sufficient.
Shift invariance, and the redundancy it implies
For any constant $a$,
Only the differences between scores matter. Two consequences:

items:
The parameters are over-determined — adding the same vector to
 every $w_c$ changes nothing. Some implementations fix one class's weights
 at zero; scikit-learn instead relies on regularisation to pin down a unique
 solution.

It gives the numerical-stability trick: subtract
 $\max_k z_k$ before exponentiating. The answer is unchanged and no
 exponential can overflow.

blocks.cap:
Left: the decision regions are still bounded by straight lines — the
 boundary between classes $i$ and $j$ is $(w_i-w_j)^{\!\top}x+(b_i-b_j)=0$, a
 hyperplane. Right: scaling all scores by $1/T$ leaves the ordering unchanged but
 sharpens or flattens the confidence.

blocks.t: The Loss and Its Gradient
Categorical cross-entropy

One-hot encode the label as $y\in\{0,1\}^{C}$ with a single 1 in position $c$.
Then

Because only one $y_{ic}$ is non-zero, this reduces per sample to
$-\log p_{i,\text{true class}}$ — the same idea as binary log loss (Topic 46),
extended to $C$ outcomes. It is again the negative log-likelihood, now of a
categorical rather than a Bernoulli distribution.
The gradient — the same clean form

Differentiating the softmax gives
$\frac{\partial p_c}{\partial z_k}=p_c(\delta_{ck}-p_k)$, and combining with the
$1/p$ from the logarithm produces an exact cancellation, exactly as in Topic 46:

Predicted minus actual, times the inputs — identical in form to linear
and binary logistic regression. The loss is convex in $W$, so gradient descent
finds the global optimum.
Softmax vs One-vs-Rest

head: Softmax (multinomial)
One-vs-Rest (OvR)
rows: Yes — raising one lowers the others
No — each is fitted in isolation
Each sub-problem is imbalanced by construction
Multi-label problems, or a base learner with no native multiclass support (e.g. SVM)

blocks.t: Which does scikit-learn use?

LogisticRegression uses multinomial softmax by default for multiclass
problems with the standard solvers. Set multi_class="ovr" for the
one-vs-rest behaviour, or wrap any binary classifier in
OneVsRestClassifier. For genuinely mutually exclusive classes, softmax is
the principled choice, because it models the fact that the probabilities must sum
to one.
Softmax assumes the classes are mutually exclusive

If an article can be tagged both "sport" and "politics", softmax is the wrong
model — it forces the probabilities to compete for a fixed total of 1. Use $C$
independent sigmoids with binary cross-entropy instead. Mutual exclusivity is a
modelling assumption, not a technicality.
Code

import numpy as np
from scipy.special import softmax as scipy_softmax, expit
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.multiclass import OneVsRestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import log_loss, accuracy_score, classification_report

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE FUNCTION -- and why we exponentiate first
# =====================================================================
def softmax(z):
    """Numerically stable: subtract the max first (shift invariance)."""
    z = np.asarray(z, dtype=float)
    e = np.exp(z - z.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    return e / e.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)

z = np.array([2.0, 4.0, 2.0])
p = softmax(z)
print("scores       :", z)
print("probabilities:", p.round(4), " sum =", p.sum())
print("matches scipy:", np.allclose(p, scipy_softmax(z)))

# Normalising the RAW scores fails as soon as one is negative:
zneg = np.array([-1.0, 3.0, -2.0])
print("\nraw normalisation:", (zneg / zneg.sum()).round(4), " <- has NEGATIVE 'probabilities'")
print("softmax          :", softmax(zneg).round(4), " <- all positive, sums to 1")

# =====================================================================
# 2. SHIFT INVARIANCE -- only the DIFFERENCES matter
# =====================================================================
for shift in [0, 10, 1000, -500]:
    print(f"softmax(z + {shift:5d}) = {softmax(z + shift).round(6)}")
# Identical every time. This is also the numerical-stability fix:
try:
    with np.errstate(over="raise"):
        naive = np.exp(np.array([1000., 1001., 999.]))
except FloatingPointError:
    print("\nnaive exp(1000) overflows")
print("stable softmax handles it:", softmax(np.array([1000., 1001., 999.])).round(4))

# =====================================================================
# 3. SOFTMAX WITH 2 CLASSES IS THE SIGMOID
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'z0':>6s} {'z1':>6s} {'softmax P(y=1)':>16s} {'sigmoid(z1-z0)':>16s}")
for z0, z1 in [(0., 1.), (2., -1.), (-3., 4.)]:
    sm = softmax(np.array([z0, z1]))[1]
    print(f"{z0:6.1f} {z1:6.1f} {sm:16.6f} {expit(z1 - z0):16.6f}")
# Identical. Binary logistic regression is softmax with one score fixed at 0.

# =====================================================================
# 4. SOFTMAX REGRESSION FROM SCRATCH
# =====================================================================
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, p_dim, C = 900, 4, 3
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, p_dim))
W_true = rng.normal(0, 1.5, (C, p_dim))
b_true = rng.normal(0, .5, C)
probs = softmax(X @ W_true.T + b_true)
y = np.array([rng.choice(C, p=row) for row in probs])

def one_hot(y, C):
    Y = np.zeros((len(y), C)); Y[np.arange(len(y)), y] = 1
    return Y

def fit_softmax(X, y, C, lr=0.5, epochs=3000):
    Xb = np.c_[X, np.ones(len(X))]              # absorb the bias
    Y  = one_hot(y, C)
    W  = np.zeros((C, Xb.shape[1]))
    for _ in range(epochs):
        P = softmax(Xb @ W.T)                   # (n, C)
        # gradient = (1/n) (P - Y)' X   -- predicted minus actual, times inputs
        W -= lr * ((P - Y).T @ Xb) / len(y)
    return W

W_hat = fit_softmax(X, y, C)
P_hat = softmax(np.c_[X, np.ones(n)] @ W_hat.T)
print(f"\nscratch accuracy : {(P_hat.argmax(1) == y).mean():.4f}")
print(f"scratch log loss : {log_loss(y, P_hat):.4f}")

sk = LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000, penalty=None).fit(X, y)
print(f"sklearn accuracy : {sk.score(X, y):.4f}")
print(f"sklearn log loss : {log_loss(y, sk.predict_proba(X)):.4f}")
# The weight MATRICES differ (shift invariance!) but the PROBABILITIES agree:
print("probabilities agree:",
      np.allclose(P_hat, sk.predict_proba(X), atol=1e-2))

# =====================================================================
# 5. THE GRADIENT, VERIFIED NUMERICALLY
# =====================================================================
Xb = np.c_[X, np.ones(n)]
Y  = one_hot(y, C)
W0 = rng.normal(0, .3, (C, Xb.shape[1]))

def loss(W):
    return -np.mean(np.sum(Y * np.log(np.clip(softmax(Xb @ W.T), 1e-12, 1)), axis=1))

analytic = ((softmax(Xb @ W0.T) - Y).T @ Xb) / n
eps = 1e-6
numeric = np.zeros_like(W0)
for i in range(C):
    for j in range(Xb.shape[1]):
        Wp = W0.copy(); Wp[i, j] += eps
        Wm = W0.copy(); Wm[i, j] -= eps
        numeric[i, j] = (loss(Wp) - loss(Wm)) / (2 * eps)
print(f"\ngradient max difference: {np.abs(analytic - numeric).max():.3e}")
# The clean (P - Y)'X form is exact -- the softmax derivative and the log's
# 1/p cancel, exactly as in the binary case.

# =====================================================================
# 6. PREDICTION -- probabilities of ALL classes, then argmax
# =====================================================================
X_new = rng.normal(0, 1, (5, p_dim))
Pn = sk.predict_proba(X_new)
print(f"\n{'':4s} {'P(c0)':>8s} {'P(c1)':>8s} {'P(c2)':>8s} {'sum':>7s} {'pick':>6s}")
for i, row in enumerate(Pn):
    print(f"{i:4d} {row[0]:8.4f} {row[1]:8.4f} {row[2]:8.4f} "
          f"{row.sum():7.4f} {row.argmax():6d}")
print("argmax matches predict():", np.array_equal(Pn.argmax(1), sk.predict(X_new)))

# =====================================================================
# 7. SOFTMAX vs ONE-VS-REST
# =====================================================================
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.3,
                                          stratify=y, random_state=0)
multi = LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
ovr   = OneVsRestClassifier(LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000)).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

print(f"\n{'model':10s} {'accuracy':>10s} {'log loss':>10s} {'row sums':>26s}")
for tag, m in [("softmax", multi), ("OvR", ovr)]:
    P = m.predict_proba(X_te)
    print(f"{tag:10s} {accuracy_score(y_te, m.predict(X_te)):10.4f} "
          f"{log_loss(y_te, P):10.4f} "
          f"{str(np.round(P.sum(1)[:3], 4)):>26s}")
# Softmax rows sum to exactly 1 by construction. OvR's are renormalised
# after the fact from three independently fitted models.

print("\nOvR fits", len(ovr.estimators_), "separate binary models;",
      "softmax fits 1 with a", multi.coef_.shape, "coefficient matrix")

# =====================================================================
# 8. MUTUAL EXCLUSIVITY IS AN ASSUMPTION
# =====================================================================
# If a sample can belong to SEVERAL classes, softmax is the wrong model --
# it forces the probabilities to compete for a fixed total of 1.
scores = np.array([3.0, 2.8, -1.0])       # first TWO labels genuinely apply
print("\nsoftmax (forced to sum to 1):", softmax(scores).round(3))
print("independent sigmoids         :", expit(scores).round(3))
# The sigmoids say "yes, yes, no" -- which is the truth. Softmax cannot
# express it, because it must divide a single unit of probability.

# =====================================================================
# 9. TEMPERATURE -- the scale of the scores IS the confidence
# =====================================================================
z = np.array([1.0, 3.0, 2.0])
print(f"\n{'T':>6s} {'probabilities':>28s}  effect")
for T in [0.25, 1.0, 4.0, 20.0]:
    eff = "sharper" if T < 1 else ("as fitted" if T == 1 else "flatter")
    print(f"{T:6.2f} {str(softmax(z / T).round(3)):>28s}  {eff}")
# argmax is unchanged for every T -- but the calibration is not. This is the
# knob used for temperature scaling and for distillation.
Worked Examples
Softmax over three classes
Linear scores (logits) for three classes: $z = [2,\;1,\;0.1]$.
Step 1 – exponentiate.
Step 2 – normalise so the outputs sum to 1.
The probabilities sum to $1.000$, and the largest logit gets the largest probability.

Step 3 – stability trick. Exponentials overflow for large logits (for example $e^{1000}$). Subtract the maximum first: $z - \max z = [0,-1,-1.9]$. The softmax is unchanged because the same constant cancels from numerator and denominator, but the numbers stay small.

Step 4 – two classes reduce to the sigmoid. With two classes and logits $[z_1, 0]$, softmax gives $p_1 = e^{z_1}/(e^{z_1}+1) = \sigma(z_1)$. Softmax regression is the multiclass generalisation of logistic regression.
Training. The loss is cross-entropy $-\sum_k y_k \log p_k$. With a one-hot label $y=[1,0,0]$ it reduces to $-\log(0.659) = 0.417$.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
Binary logistic regression handles $\{0,1\}$; now we have more
 than 2 classes, e.g. Yes / No / Opt-out.

For each class the model computes a score $z_1,z_2,z_3$.
 Softmax converts these scores to probabilities between 0 and 1,
 and we pick the class with the highest probability.

$P(y=c\mid x)=\dfrac{e^{z_c}}{\sum_k e^{z_k}}$. Exponentiating makes every
 term positive; dividing by the sum forces the total to 1.

With $C=2$, softmax reduces exactly to $\sigma(z_1-z_0)$ — the
 sigmoid is the two-class special case.

Shift invariance: adding a constant to every score changes
 nothing. This makes the parameters over-determined, and gives the
 stability trick of subtracting $\max_k z_k$ before exponentiating.

Loss: categorical cross-entropy
 $-\frac1n\sum_i\sum_c y_{ic}\log p_{ic}$, which reduces to
 $-\log p_{\text{true class}}$ per sample.

Gradient: $\frac1n(P-Y)^{\!\top}X$ — predicted minus actual,
 times the inputs, the same clean form as linear and binary logistic
 regression. The loss is convex.
Decision regions are still bounded by straight lines.

Softmax assumes the classes are mutually exclusive. For
 multi-label problems use independent sigmoids instead.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. What does softmax do and why exponentiate?

It converts $C$ real-valued scores into a probability distribution. The
exponential makes every value positive regardless of the score's sign — raw
normalisation would produce negative "probabilities" — and dividing by the sum
forces the total to 1. It also amplifies score differences, which is why it
approximates a hard maximum smoothly.
Q. How does softmax relate to the sigmoid?

The sigmoid is softmax with two classes. Dividing through by $e^{z_1}$ gives
$P(y=1)=\sigma(z_1-z_0)$. Binary logistic regression fixes one score at zero and
keeps a single weight vector, which is why it needs only one.
Q. Why subtract the maximum before exponentiating?

Because softmax is shift-invariant — adding a constant to every score leaves the
output unchanged — so subtracting the maximum is free and guarantees the largest
exponent is $e^0=1$. Without it, a score of 1000 overflows to inf and the
result becomes nan.
Q. What is the gradient of softmax with cross-entropy?

$\frac1n(P-Y)^{\!\top}X$ — predicted minus actual, times the inputs. The
softmax Jacobian and the logarithm's $1/p$ cancel exactly, which is why the
softmax/cross-entropy pairing is standard rather than accidental.
Q. Softmax or one-vs-rest?

Softmax when the classes are mutually exclusive: it fits one joint model whose
probabilities sum to 1 by construction and whose classes genuinely compete. OvR
when you need a base learner without native multiclass support, or when the
problem is multi-label — in which case softmax is simply the wrong model.
Q. Can a single sample belong to two classes under softmax?

No, and that is the assumption. The probabilities are forced to sum to 1, so
raising one lowers the others. For multi-label problems use $C$ independent
sigmoids with binary cross-entropy.
Q. Are softmax decision boundaries linear?

Yes. The boundary between classes $i$ and $j$ is where $z_i=z_j$, i.e. 
$(w_i-w_j)^{\!\top}x+(b_i-b_j)=0$ — a hyperplane. The regions are convex
polytopes. Curved boundaries require transformed features (Topic 51).
